title: Serum Institute Is Racing to Build an Ebola Vaccine in 30 Days. The Same Factory Made a Billion COVID Shots.
excerpt: With 900 cases and 220 deaths from a strain with no approved vaccine, India's vaccine giant deploys the same Oxford platform that powered Covishield against Bundibugyo Ebola.
body:
The Serum Institute of India, the world's largest vaccine manufacturer, has entered a race against time to produce a vaccine for the deadliest Ebola outbreak in years. Partnering with the University of Oxford and the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, SII is deploying the same ChAdOx1 viral-vector technology that powered the Oxford-AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine — a platform its production lines already know by heart.

## 900 Cases, 220 Deaths, No Approved Vaccine

The Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus has now infected more than 900 people and killed at least 220 across the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda, according to the World Health Organization. The WHO has declared the outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention has classified it a Public Health Emergency of Continental Security.

There is no licensed vaccine and no approved therapy for the Bundibugyo strain. The existing Ebola vaccine — Merck's Ervebo — was designed for the Zaire strain and should not be deployed outside research settings against Bundibugyo, the WHO said Thursday.

## India's 20-to-30-Day Sprint

SII says it can begin producing vaccine doses in as little as 20 to 30 days. An SII spokesperson told the Mint that the moment the company received word of the Bundibugyo outbreak, it activated its emergency response framework.

"Oxford's master viral seed will allow us to rapidly inoculate our cell bank and begin producing vaccine doses in record time," the spokesperson said. "This is exactly the kind of agility India's biopharmaceutical sector brings to the world. The ChAdOx1 vector platform is well understood by our teams, and we are fully prepared to scale."

The ChAdOx1 platform — which uses a weakened chimpanzee adenovirus to carry genetic instructions into human cells — has already proven its speed. During the COVID-19 pandemic, SII manufactured over a billion doses of the Oxford-AstraZeneca vaccine under its Covishield brand, supplying much of the developing world.

## The WHO's Three-Track Strategy

The WHO recommended on Thursday that three experimental treatments should be prioritised for clinical trials: Mapp Biopharmaceutical's MBP134, Regeneron's maftivimab, and Gilead Sciences' remdesivir. For prevention, Gilead's experimental oral antiviral obeldesivir was highlighted for post-exposure use.

Among vaccine candidates, the most advanced is a single-dose vaccine called rVSV Bundibugyo, being developed by the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative. But it will not be ready for trials for another seven to nine months.

The Oxford-SII ChAdOx1 Bundibugyo vaccine could be available for testing within two to three months, making it the nearest-term candidate for deployment — though the WHO stressed that additional animal data are still needed before clinical trials can begin.

## India's Domestic Preparedness

Union Health Minister **J.P. Nadda** has reviewed national preparedness measures and ordered screening at all airports, seaports, and land border crossings to remain at heightened levels. The Indian Council of Medical Research and the National Centre for Disease Control have placed diagnostic laboratories in a state of readiness.

A woman arriving in Bengaluru from Uganda was quarantined this week as a precaution, though India has reported no confirmed cases of the Bundibugyo strain. The Directorate General of Health Services has issued a travel advisory requiring any incoming passenger from the DRC, Uganda, or South Sudan with symptoms such as fever, vomiting, or unexplained bleeding to report immediately to a health officer before crossing immigration.

Delhi airport has implemented non-contact thermal screening, designated transit corridors, and mandatory health self-declaration forms for travellers arriving from affected regions.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, the outbreak has two dimensions. The first is personal safety — thousands of Indians live and work across East and Central Africa, and the India-Africa corridor is one of the busiest travel routes for NRIs in the Gulf and the subcontinent. The India-Africa Forum Summit, scheduled for this week in New Delhi, has been postponed over public health concerns.

The second is institutional significance: India's ability to manufacture vaccines at speed and scale, demonstrated during COVID-19 when SII supplied over 170 countries, is now being tested again in a different crisis with even less warning. If the ChAdOx1 Bundibugyo vaccine proves effective, it would underscore India's position as the world's pharmacy — a role that has become central to the country's global identity and soft power.
